turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Sunday, the thirteenth of September, twenty twenty-six. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three things on the table this morning. A second oil gate is contested — and then, on Friday, a door opens in Oman.
A family in India pawns the gold on its wrist without a trace of shame. We'll get to why that's the biggest story in the book.
And model railways. [wry] Yes, really. The oval on the table that quietly becomes a whole world.
[amused] I'm weirdly excited about the trains, Claire. But start me with the war.
The map closed further before it cracked. On Friday the Houthis seized Perim — the island in the throat of the Bab-el-Mandeb strait — a day after taking the port of Mocha.
So that's the Red Sea gate. And Hormuz, on the other side of Arabia, is still a shooting war.
Both doors to the Gulf's oil, contested at once. A pincer.
[thoughtful] How do you even measure that on a normal Friday?
The flow. Transits through Bab-el-Mandeb halved — fifteen ships against thirty the day before. The market's pricing a managed closure, not a single strike.
Okay. So where's the door that opened?
Iranian state media said Tehran will meet the Gulf states in Muscat, in Oman, on Monday, to talk about a temporary arrangement for shipping through Hormuz.
The first real de-escalation signal since February.

And the price listened. Brent had closed above a hundred dollars for the first time since May, then gave back nearly three per cent on the talks — settling at a hundred and four dollars and sixty-one cents.
Two ways to read the same week. What did the viewpoint panels say?

Al Jazeera, out of Doha, files it as a US-Israel war on Iran — the strait stays shut until the war is settled, not bombed. Fox, in New York, calls it an Iran-backed terror grab menacing a second chokepoint, and makes the case for force.
[thoughtful] Same fifteen ships. Two completely different stories.
The Chatter reads Friday's fade as the market pricing Monday's talks, not any single event on the water. The war premium is reversible the moment the oil actually flows again.
So the live risk isn't a headline. It's the halved transits.

The halved transits. And here's the sceptic, because the oil bulls are fighting the forecasters. The US Energy Information Administration still models Brent around ninety dollars in the back half of the year.
Meaning the premium fades the moment the oil actually flows.
Goldman only sees a hundred and twenty next year, and only if Gulf output stays about four million barrels a day below where it was. That's a condition, not a forecast.
Right. Anything else moving in the world before we talk money?

Ukraine's short truce lapsed on schedule — Russia hit Kyiv, Putin rejected any front-line pause. The delta was European money, not diplomacy: Brussels approved another seven billion euros for air defence.
[sighs] Planning for a long war, then.
Planning for a long war. Which brings us to the money block — because the same dear money runs under everything this week.
Lay it out for me. What's the one force?
An oil-shock reflation meeting a Fed that's expected to raise rates, not cut, when it meets this week. Markets put the odds of a hike anywhere from seventy to ninety per cent.
A hike. Into an oil spike. That's a chain reaction.

It is a chain, not a list. War premium in oil feeds an inflation scare; a Fed leaning to tighten pushes the ten-year Treasury yield toward five per cent; a firm yield keeps the dollar bid; and a firm dollar leans on everything else.
So read it through the four instruments for me. Global stocks first.
A twin headwind — rates and oil — with a hawkish hike the live risk. Global bonds are capped while a five-per-cent ten-year is the anchor.
And gold? Gold's been on a tear.
Gold's bid — the war and inflation hedge — but range-bound near four thousand three hundred and eighty-five dollars, still under its January record around five thousand five hundred and eighty-nine.
Bitcoin?
Trading as a risk asset. Soft into the meeting, around seventy-seven thousand, and running an unusually high correlation with gold right now. And to be clear — that's explanation, not advice.
[thoughtful] Hold that thought on gold. It comes back at the very end, and it's the whole issue.
It does. Closer to home — the haze. Singapore's first unhealthy reading since twenty twenty-three, and then Friday's rain pulled the air back to the healthy band across all five regions.
So the weekend's saved. Mostly.
Mostly. The dry spell isn't finished — hazy days may recur into October — so check the dashboard before the outdoor hours, not the calendar.
And there was a pay-rise row, wasn't there?

The Workers' Party backed the one-off raise of up to nine per cent, but pressed the one demand that bites — disclose ministers' actual total remuneration. The number sharpening it: a median gross income of five thousand seven hundred and seventy-five dollars a month.
The argument turned on a single word. Disclosure. [wry] I like that.
Now — technology, and the summit clock is ticking. Xi flies to Washington in a fortnight, and Nvidia's China business is the top item.
There was a deal to sell them the H-two-hundred chips, wasn't there? With Washington taking a cut.
A quarter of the proceeds. And it's delivering almost nothing — Beijing restricted the purchases, so Nvidia has excluded China from its outlook entirely.
Because China's building its own.
Fast. Huawei laid out an Ascend roadmap, and DeepSeek reportedly ordered a hundred and sixty thousand of the coming parts for a single data centre in Inner Mongolia.
[exhales] A hundred and sixty thousand. That's a wall of silicon.
The sceptic's note: those performance numbers are Huawei's own, not independent benchmarks, and the real ceiling is still software parity with Nvidia, not raw specs.
Okay, but the bit our home-lab listeners actually care about — anything new to run this week?
DeepSeek dropped a new open-weights model, V-four-point-one Flash, under a permissive licence. Five hundred and fifty-two billion parameters, but only eight to sixteen active at a time.
[curious] Meaning it's big but fast, because most of the brain is asleep between words.

Exactly. A three-bit build fits in about a hundred and three gigabytes — runnable on a serious desktop. And two new boxes at the show can hold it: a Grace-Blackwell Spark, and a Minisforum with a hundred and ninety-two gigabytes of unified memory.
There's a catch. There's always a catch.
The bottleneck is memory bandwidth, not capacity. It'll load the model; the question is tokens-per-second on long context. Buy the memory, not the marketing.
Now, The Kit — and I actually love this one, because it argues our whole religion.
Beyerdynamic's Aventho Y — a wireless headphone you can actually repair. User-replaceable battery, magnetic ear cushions, ninety hours of play, about a hundred and fifty US dollars.
[warmly] A wireless can that doesn't become landfill the day the battery dies. That's the buy-once idea moved to a gadget.
The sceptic: repairable is only worth paying for if the parts still exist in three years. Ask whether they stock the battery a decade out, not whether the hatch opens today.
Fair. And the maker of the day — the Atelier — what did we take apart?
A suit. And here's the one thing that lets you judge any jacket on any rack, cold — how the chest is built. Fused is glued, and it bubbles. Full-canvas floats, and it moulds to you over years.
How do I tell, standing in the shop?
The pinch test. At the front hem, pinch the wool and lining and rub. Three layers moving freely — it's canvassed. One stiff board — it's glued.
[amused] I'm going to be doing that in every shop now. What about the fabric numbers — the Super hundred-and-fifties?
Marketing. Higher just means finer, more delicate, shorter-lived. The number that matters is the weight — in Singapore, buy a light, high-twist fresco, and you need one or two, not a wardrobe.
And who really makes them?
The white-label truth: one Italian mill, Vitale Barberis Canonico, weaves about half its cloth under other brands' names. Buy the maker, not the logo.
[wry] Buy the maker, not the logo. Put that on a T-shirt. Okay — [warmly] right. Take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every week with this one.
[laughs] Model railways, Claire. Sell me on it in one sentence.

It's four hobbies wearing one set of tracks — engineering, craft, collecting and operations — and the gateway is the same for everyone: a locomotive that starts slowly, crawls at a walking pace, and makes engine sound. The oval stops being a toy and becomes a place.
And there's a whole world down there.

A deep one — and a greying one. The free magazine has an audience near seventy-seven thousand; but the American national body put its members' average age at sixty-four, up from thirty-nine in the seventies. That tension runs through the whole thing.
So where does a normal person start — without buying a basement?
A quality starter set — a Kato in the small scale, or a Hornby — plus decent track. Skip the supermarket toy oval; it's a dead end. And decide your scale before you spend a cent.
[curious] And the top of the mountain? Because there's always a mountain.

Brass. Locomotives hand-built in Korea, imported one run at a time, often bought to own rather than run — well into four figures. And a finescale tier so exact the joke is that its devotees can't keep the wheels on their own track.
[gasps] Four figures, for one model train.

And here's the bit made for you — the tech-forward pick. An open-source project called DCC-EX runs a full command station on a cheap Arduino board, and turns your phone into the throttle. The maker's way into a hobby everyone thinks is your grandad's.
[warmly] Okay, that I did not see coming. An Arduino running a railway.

But the sceptic is the community itself, and it's honest. A layout is a money pit that's never finished, and most people never get the room — a board the size of a briefcase is the smallest scale only.
So what's the secret they tell the overspenders?

[thoughtful] That the digital control everyone chases is a want, not a need, on a small layout — for one locomotive on an oval, plain old direct current does fine. Buy the model that runs, not the one that gleams in a cabinet.
[chuckles] I did not expect the train segment to end on restraint. Alright — culture and the body, quickly. Venice.
The Golden Lion went to Woman Unknown, a Danish thriller by May el-Toukhy — and its lead, Mathilde Arcel, took Best Actress too, a rare double.
And didn't we call one of these?

[wry] We did. We said in issue ninety-eight the Lion would not go to Martin McDonagh's Wild Horse Nine. It didn't — though John Malkovich took Best Actor for it. We'll grade it properly next Saturday.
[amused] A quiet victory lap. I'll allow it. And there was music too, wasn't there?
Kasabian's ninth, and — this is the one for our vinyl listeners — Neil Young's fiftieth studio album, out this week. Eighty years old, still cutting to tape.
[warmly] Fiftieth. What a run. Okay — The Good Life?

Citizen's Eco-Drive turns fifty — the watch that runs on any light and never needs winding or a battery. The anniversary piece sets a hand-dyed Japanese-paper dial in titanium, for three thousand and ninety-five dollars.
The opposite of the wind-it-yourself religion, and just as pure.
A thing engineered to ask nothing of you. And the Family Desk — Singapore's age-assurance law arrives in twenty twenty-seven: under-thirteens blocked, curbs on the endless scroll.
But the evidence is messier than the headline, right?
Much. A big study this year found school phone bans had roughly zero average effect on test scores. Even the alarming screen-time study found the harm ran through sleep and physical activity.
[thoughtful] So the mechanism is the lever. Guard the bedtime, protect the sport.
Guard the bedtime first — it's the firmest evidence there is. General guidance, not medical advice. And on Fitness — grip strength.
A handshake predicts your decade. I've heard Attia say that.
A study this year found the strongest-grip group had about a third lower risk of death. And the honest twist: Zone-two cardio is a base, not a magic bullet — you still need some hard intervals.
[warmly] Hang from a bar and count. I can do that. Quick one for the Diary?

The Singapore Grand Prix, the ninth to eleventh of October, with the season's first-ever Sprint — track action every day. And a marquee to fly for: the Sapporo Snow Festival in February, with snow slides built for a twelve-year-old.
Book the flights now.
Book the flights now.
[exhales] Okay. Take us home, Claire. The Long Read — and you promised gold comes back.
[drawn out] It does. In a slower register now. There's a word in India — streedhan. A woman's own gold, gifted at marriage or passed mother to daughter. Legally, culturally, hers.
And the rule was you never touched it.

The rule was you never touched it. To pawn the family jewellery — above all the marriage necklace — was a mark of ruin. That rule is dissolving. Not in the dark. Loudly, on television, sold as smart finance.
[thoughtful] How big is this, really?
Indian households hold something like thirty-four thousand six hundred tonnes of gold — nearly ninety per cent of the country's entire economy. And the loans against it more than doubled in a year.
And it's women at the centre of it.
Women hold about forty-three-and-a-half per cent of the gold loans — the highest share of any credit product in India. Higher than education loans, higher than home loans.
[whispers] There's a history here, isn't there. The country did this once.

In nineteen ninety-one, in a balance-of-payments crisis, India pledged sixty-seven tonnes of gold to raise a couple of billion dollars — some of it flown out in secret, at night, because the shame of a nation pawning its gold risked a panic.
[exhales] And now the whole country does it in daylight. Without the shame.

That's the essay's spine. The state did once, in the dark, exactly what tens of millions of households now do routinely, on camera. The distance travelled isn't economic — it's cultural. And it was engineered: a lender ran a whole campaign, narrated by Amitabh Bachchan, built to break the shame of pledging.
So is it good news or bad news? Agency, or distress?
[thoughtful] The honest answer is both, at once. It's a real asset finally put to work — and it's a family reaching for its last line because the month ran short. The same bracelet.
And that ties back to gold's record run everywhere else.

That's the thread of the whole issue. When both the central bank and the citizen quietly load up on the oldest reserve there is, they're answering the same question about the future — in the same direction.
[warmly] The reserve. That's the word, isn't it — for the whole book.

It is. The gold in the vault, the gold on the wrist. The suit and the little railway built to outlast us. The buy-once desks are the same question answered by owning less, better. Seneca had it in nine words: it is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.
[exhales] That's a place to stop.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
